text.hook:
std::thread looks simple.
Interviewers use it to test lifetime, ownership and argument passing.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Two objects, two lifetimes
2. What joinable() really means
3. How arguments reach the thread
4. Exceptions and jthread
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: `Task` is a function object. Does `std::thread t(Task());` start a thread? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. Most vexing parse: it declares a function named t, so t.join() fails to compile. Write std::thread t{Task{}}; instead.

slides.lead: Lifetime, joinable() and argument passing: what interviewers actually check.

slides.title: Two objects, two separate lifetimes

cards.label: Thread of execution
cards.text: The OS thread that runs your callable.

cards.label: std::thread object
cards.text: An owning handle to it, like `std::unique_ptr`. Move-only: one owner joins.

slides.takeaway: Before the handle dies: `join()` (wait) or `detach()` (give up ownership). Forget, and the destructor calls `std::terminate()`.

slides.title: What `joinable()` really tracks
slides.takeaway: `joinable()` means "owns an unjoined, undetached thread", not "is running".

slides.title: What is guaranteed, and when
steps: `f` and `args` are copied **in the creating thread**
the constructor returns: the new thread may not have run anything yet
`join()` returns: every write the worker made is visible

slides.title: Decay-copied, then passed as rvalues
slides.takeaway: `char buf[]` is copied as a pointer. Convert first: `std::thread t(f, std::string(buf));`

cards.label: Escapes the worker
cards.text: `std::terminate()`. Never delivered to the thread that joins.

cards.label: Transport it
cards.text: Catch, store `std::current_exception()`, `std::rethrow_exception` after `join()`. Or use a future.

cards.label: Creator throws first
cards.text: Unwinding destroys a joinable `t`: terminate. Use a join guard or `std::jthread`.

slides.lead: The `jthread` destructor calls `request_stop()`, then `join()`. The worker must check its `stop_token` and return.

items.myth: "The worker already finished, so destroying the `std::thread` is fine."
items.truth: The destructor checks `joinable()`, not "still running". Unjoined means terminate.
It calls `std::terminate()`. There is nothing to catch.

items.myth: "Passing `value` to an `int&` parameter creates a temporary that dangles."
"A `const T&` parameter sees the caller's variable."
items.truth: It sees the thread's private copy unless you pass `std::ref`.

items.myth: "`detach()` makes the thread safe and independent."
items.truth: It only removes the owner. Every lifetime problem is still yours.

items.myth: "A `bool` stop flag is atomic on x86, so it is fine."
items.truth: Unsynchronized read + write is a data race: UB in C++, on any hardware.

slides.hero:
Every `std::thread`:
join it or detach it.

Every argument:
copied, unless `std::ref`.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The worker thread finished 100 ms ago.
So leaving main is safe, right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One of the most common std::thread bugs. The fix is one line, but the reason is what interviewers ask about.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: you call `t.join()` twice on the same thread. What happens on the second call? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: The second join() throws std::system_error (invalid_argument), because t is no longer joinable. Unlike destroying a joinable thread, this is a catchable exception.

slides.title:
The worker finishes long before main ends.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: libstdc++: "terminate called without an active exception", abort
bullets: `t` was never joined or detached.
`~thread()` checks `joinable()`, not "still running". It is still `true`.
Finished thread + unjoined handle = joinable = terminate.
Extra trap: `abort()` does not flush stdio. Piped to a file, both lines may vanish.

slides.tip: C++20 `std::jthread` joins in its destructor, so this bug cannot happen.
slides.takeaway: Finishing the thread does not make the `std::thread` object non-joinable. Only `join()`, `detach()` or a move do.

text.hook:
Four lines. One detach(). One [&].
Is this code safe?

Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: It can print 42 on one machine and garbage on the next. The output does not answer the question.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: four threads are created in a loop with `[&] { std::cout << i; }` and joined after the loop. What is wrong? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: All four lambdas share the same loop variable i: main's ++i races with their reads (UB), and i dies after the loop while threads may still read it. Capture [i] by value.

slides.title: Is this code safe?
options: Yes: the new thread starts running immediately.
No: `foo()` may return and destroy `value` first.
Yes: the thread stores its own copy of the lambda.
Yes, if it prints 42 in testing.

slides.verdict_sub: Detached thread + `[&]` capture of a local = dangling reference
bullets: `[&]` stores a **reference** to `value`, not a copy.
After `detach()`, `foo()` can return and destroy `value`.
A read after that is undefined behaviour, even if it prints 42.
Fixes: capture `[value]`, `join()` before returning, or pass owning data.
slides.cta: Why not A, C or D ➜

items: A: no guarantee the new thread has run anything when the constructor returns.
C: the lambda is stored in the thread, but its `[&]` capture still refers to `foo`'s stack.
D: a passing test proves nothing. In practice `foo()` usually returns before the thread even starts.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "`detach()` plus `[&]` is almost always a bug. ASan reports `stack-use-after-return` when that detection is enabled."

text.hook:
A thread, a lambda taking int&, and a plain int.
What does this program print?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This is the question behind every std::ref you have ever written.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: `obj` is a `Worker` with a member function `run(int)`. How do you start a std::thread that runs `obj.run(42)` without writing a lambda? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: `std::thread t(&Worker::run, &obj, 42);` member pointer, then object pointer, then the arguments (std::invoke rules). `&obj` is non-owning, so obj must outlive the thread.

slides.title:
Does this compile?
If yes, what does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: libstdc++: "std::thread arguments must be invocable after conversion to rvalues"
bullets: `std::thread` stores a **copy** of `value`.
It passes that copy to the lambda as an **rvalue**.
An rvalue cannot bind to a non-const `int&`.
No silent binding to a hidden copy, nothing dangles. It just fails.
slides.wrong: "43, then 42" (a reference to a hidden copy)

slides.title: `std::ref` vs `const int&`

columns.label: const int&

slides.takeaway: `std::thread` never keeps references implicitly. Want the original? Pass `std::ref`, and keep the object alive.

text.hook:
8 cores. Purely CPU-bound work.
How many threads do you start?

Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: The "obvious" answer is only half right. The other half is what makes it a senior answer.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up an interviewer would ask next: "Why not create a new std::thread for each of 10,000 tasks per second?" Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Each create+join costs tens of microseconds (clone, stack mapping, TLS setup, scheduling) and thousands of threads oversubscribe the CPUs. Use a fixed pool of long-lived workers fed by a queue.

slides.title: Purely CPU-bound tasks on 8 cores. How many worker threads?
options: 100 or more: more threads, more parallelism.
About one per available logical CPU, then benchmark.

slides.verdict: D. One per available logical CPU, then measure
slides.verdict_sub: A starting point, not a law
bullets: N logical CPUs execute at most N threads at the same time.
Extra threads add context switches, cache and TLB pollution, preempted lock holders.
With SMT, 8 logical CPUs may be only 4 physical cores.
I/O-bound work differs: blocked threads leave the CPU free.
slides.cta: Why not A, B or C ➜

items: A: more threads never add CPU capacity. The OS just time-slices them.
B: memory bandwidth, SMT, contention and other load move the optimum. Measure.
C: it is a hint. It may return 0, and on Linux ignores affinity masks and container CPU quotas.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "For latency-critical work, pin a small number of threads to isolated cores and avoid oversubscription entirely."

text.hook:
main reads *ptr only after join().
join() synchronizes everything. So this is correct?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Two separate questions hide in this program. Most answers only check one of them.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: `t` still owns an unjoined thread, and you write `t = std::thread(g);`. What happens? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: std::terminate(), exactly like destroying a joinable thread: move assignment does not join the old one. Join or detach first (std::jthread instead requests stop and joins).

slides.title:
`*ptr` is read after `join()`.
Is this correct?

slides.verdict_sub: `ptr` points to a destroyed object: 42, garbage or a crash
bullets: `value` dies when `worker()` **returns**, before `join()` returns.
The write to `ptr` is fine: thread completion synchronizes-with `join()`.
So no data race on `ptr`. The object it points to is just dead.
`join()` waits. It never extends the worker's locals.

slides.title: Let the longer-lived thread own the object
slides.takeaway: Synchronization and object lifetime are separate questions. A correct answer checks both.
